Within Chapter 6’s scope—hot and cold water-supply systems for use in connection with human occupancy and habitation, and installation of individual water-supply systems—if pressure within a building exceeds **85 psi (586 kPa) static**, an approved valve conforming to ASSE 1003 or CSA B356, with a strainer, must reduce pressure in the building water-distribution piping to **85 psi (586 kPa) static or less** (PC §§ 601.1, 604.8).

Section 604.8 excepts **service lines to sill cocks and outside hydrants**, and **main supply risers where pressure from the mains is reduced to 85 psi (586 kPa) or less at individual fixtures**. The fixture-pressure condition qualifies the main-supply-riser exception; it is not a blanket exception for all risers.

cases.answerText: **No.** PC § 604.8 requires pressure reduction when pressure within a building **exceeds** 85 psi static; exactly 85 psi is the limit, not above it. On your stated facts, that pressure alone does not trigger the requirement. The section’s exceptions are for service lines to sill cocks and outside hydrants, and for main supply risers where mains pressure is reduced to 85 psi or less at individual fixtures; neither is needed for this conclusion. Chapter 6 governs the covered hot- and cold-water supply systems described in PC § 601.1.

Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, **where an enclosure is not required**, grease-duct systems and exhaust equipment serving a Type I hood must be at least **18 in. (457.2 mm) from combustible construction** and **3 in. (76.2 mm) from noncombustible construction and gypsum wallboard attached to noncombustible structures** (MC § 506.3.6). Chapter 5 governs mechanical exhaust systems, including those serving cooking appliances (MC § 501.1). MC § 202 defines “clearance” as the minimum distance through air from the heat-producing surface of the appliance, device, or equipment to combustible material or an assembly.

The stated exceptions are:
- **Factory-built grease duct:** If listed and labeled under UL 1978, its clearance is the one in its listing, subject to commissioner approval.
- **Listed exhaust equipment:** Listed and labeled exhaust equipment installed under MC § 304.1 is excepted. Section 304.1 requires installation according to the terms of approval, listing conditions, manufacturer’s instructions, and the code; § 506.3.6 does not give this exception a replacement numerical clearance.
- **Field-applied enclosure:** If the grease duct is continuously covered on all sides by listed and labeled field-applied enclosure material, a system, product, or method specifically evaluated for this purpose under ASTM E 2336, clearance follows that listing.
- **Specified insulation:** Grease ducts with at least 2 in. (50.8 mm) of magnesium- or calcium-silicate block insulation, staggered joints, and attachment by galvanized steel wire—or by a material assembly equivalent in insulating and fire-resistant qualities and not penetrable by grease—are excepted from the stated minima. This protection must be applied to all ducts inside the building and approved by the commissioner. This exception gives no alternate numerical clearance.

A clearance exception does **not** itself waive a separate enclosure requirement. A commercial-kitchen grease duct serving a Type I hood that penetrates a ceiling, wall, floor, or concealed space must be enclosed from its first penetration to the outlet terminal; the stated exception is a duct that penetrates only a nonfire-resistance-rated roof/ceiling assembly (MC § 506.3.11). Although MC § 506.3.11.3 specifies UL 2221 for factory-built grease-duct enclosure assemblies, MC § 506.3.6’s express factory-built clearance exception specifies UL 1978; UL 2221 alone is not identified there as a substitute clearance.

cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, where an enclosure is not required, a grease-duct system serving a Type I hood must be at least **18 inches from combustible construction**. At **3 inches**, the stated clearance is insufficient (MC § 506.3.6). You’ve stipulated that no listed-system or insulation exception applies, so none changes that result.

Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, a means-of-egress ramp must meet the corridor minimum width and required capacity, and must also have at least 36 inches (914.4 mm) of clear width between handrails, if provided, or other permissible projections. The referenced corridor-capacity calculation is in BC § 1005, so its method cannot be explained from the text available here. (BC §§ 1012.5.1, 1020.2)

- **Corridor minimum widths:** Table 1020.2 states values in inches: 44 for facilities not listed below; 24 for access to and utilization of mechanical, plumbing, or electrical systems or equipment; 36 for occupant loads of 50 or less, except as otherwise required by Chapter 11; 36 within dwelling units in Groups I-1 and R-1, except as otherwise required by § 1107; and 30 within dwelling units in Groups R-2 and R-3, except as otherwise required by § 1107. The other listed values are 66 for Group E corridors serving classrooms; 72 for corridors and areas serving stretcher traffic where outpatient medical care makes patients incapable of self-preservation; and 96 for Group I-2 areas where required for bed movement. For Group I-2, 96 inches of clear width is not required in areas without stretcher or bed movement for access to care or as part of the defend-in-place strategy. The ramp must satisfy the applicable corridor minimum as well as its separate 36-inch clear-width minimum. (BC §§ 1012.5.1, 1020.2)
- **Headroom:** At least 84 inches (2133.6 mm) in all parts of the ramp. (BC § 1012.5.2)
- **Width reductions and doors:** A means-of-egress ramp must not reduce in width in the direction of egress travel; projections into required ramp or landing width are prohibited. A door opening onto a landing must not reduce clear width below 42 inches (1066.8 mm). (BC § 1012.5.3)
- **Landing width:** At least the width of the widest adjoining ramp run. (BC § 1012.6.2)

cases.gradingLimit: Existing exposed rubric, implementing-assistant review; not independent accuracy evidence.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Exactly 84 inches meets the 2022 NYC Building Code minimum: headroom in all parts of a means-of-egress ramp must be at least 84 inches (BC § 1012.5.2).
